The key distinction between the Panel and the Appellate Body lies in their interpretation of **Article 19.3 of the SCM Agreement** and the concept of "double remedies" (i.e., the simultaneous application of anti-dumping and countervailing duties on the same product). The **Panel** initially concluded that China had not demonstrated that the U.S. measures were inconsistent with Article 19.3 because it interpreted the provision as being **silent on the issue of double remedies**, and that the **NME methodology** used by the U.S. did not necessarily lead to an "excess" in countervailing duties. The **Appellate Body**, however, **reversed this interpretation**, finding that the Panel had failed to consider the broader context of the SCM Agreement and the **interplay between countervailing and anti-dumping duties**.

The Appellate Body reasoned that the term "appropriate amounts" in Article 19.3 should not be read in isolation but must be interpreted **in the context of the Anti-Dumping Agreement** and the **object and purpose of the SCM Agreement**. It emphasized that **double remedies are not inherently prohibited** in the SCM Agreement and that the U.S. approach, which used a **non-market economy methodology** (NME), might have **overlooked the cumulative effect of subsidies**. The Appellate Body argued that the **Panel's interpretation was overly rigid** and did not adequately account for the **collective legal framework** of the WTO agreements, suggesting that the "appropriate amount" of countervailing duties must be judged holistically, taking into consideration both **subsidies and the injury** they cause.

Thus, the **Panel**'s findings were based on a **narrow reading of the SCM Agreement**, while the **Appellate Body** adopted a **more comprehensive, context-driven interpretation**, recognizing that **double remedies could be inconsistent** with the obligation to ensure that duties are "appropriate" in light of the **collective application** of anti-dumping and countervailing measures.
